flawed_step: Lines 31 and 35–37 incorrectly claim that both strategies have the same cost in every RR case and that dispatching the closest ambulance is globally optimal.
counterexample: Put A,B at 0 and C at 1. If the first incident is at 0.6 and the second at 0.9, closest-first sends C then A/B, costing 0.4+0.9=1.3. Sending A first and C second costs 0.6+0.1=0.7, directly contradicting line 35. More strongly, use the policy: for the first incident t, send a left ambulance when t<=5/8 and C otherwise; then send the nearest remaining ambulance. Its expected total distance for two incidents is integral_0^(5/8)(t+1/4)dt + integral_(5/8)^1(3/2-t)dt = 39/64. Closest-first has expected total 1/4 + (1/2)(1/4) + (1/2)(1/2) = 5/8 = 40/64. Thus the threshold policy strictly improves the average.
assessment_summary: The proof's payoff table suppresses distances within each half. In RR cases, the two strategies do not generally have equal costs, and exploiting the first incident's exact position yields an explicit policy with lower expected total response distance than closest-first.
